prize_parts.citation: for building a formal and empirically testable political economics of how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged after round 1 and the chair's questions, but my reasoning is more qualified. The core claim is that Persson, Tabellini and Besley made government an endogenous actor. Electoral rules, forms of government, accountability and state capacity became objects of formal analysis that produce testable predictions about fiscal policy and public-goods provision. The empirical tests use both cross-country and within-country variation. The contribution is a framework with a long record of extension. It is about 25 to 30 years old, and the field has had time to challenge and refine it, so maturity is not a concern. Credit is reasonably concentrated: Persson and Tabellini for the constitutions and electoral-rules programme and its synthesis, and Besley for state capacity and political agency, with joint work among all three. I have also tested my own preference against the criterion the B001 supporters use, which is credit by origin of the idea. By that criterion Persson and Tabellini are the originators for the constitutional programme. Besley's state-capacity strand is a separable, complementary originating contribution, not a later extension. I still weigh B006's attribution as somewhat easier to defend than B001's, but I now see the gap as narrower than I said in round 1. My own rule is to judge a prize by the specific scientific contribution and the credibility of its evidence, and the citation I draft is worded around the framework and its testable predictions, not around settled causal effects of particular constitutions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is identification. The constitutional and electoral-rule effects rest mostly on cross-country observational variation, which is weaker than the design-based evidence I am used to in labour and crime economics. Every B006 supporter concedes this, and the citation should not claim more than the framework supports. The second reservation is the 2024 institutions prize. I read the two programmes as distinct, but that is a judgement and not an established fact, and it may not survive if the committee thinks the evidence is thin. The third is that Besley's separability is contested. The chair and Boppart named only Persson and Tabellini in their openings, and a two-person prize is a defensible fallback. The fourth is that B006 has three explicit supporters and cannot reach six votes without drawing on members who now prefer B001, B002 or B021. I do not treat that as evidence about merit, but it affects what the committee can realistically decide.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first. He argues that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are origin points (pricing device, contracts and rule, normative synthesis). He says Galí, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum mostly codified, estimated and extended that structure, and that the post-2021 inflation tested the framework without breaking it.
responses.response: This is the clearest answer to the chair's question on B001, and it moves me part of the way. My reservation was that any trio leaves out people with strong claims. If the criterion is origin of the idea and not estimation or adoption, then the trio is separable, and my attribution worry about B001 is smaller than in round 1. I cannot judge the macro literature as well as he can, and two questions are still open to me. One is how priority among Calvo, Taylor, Fischer and Phelps is resolved. The other is whether a prize for origin points would be read as passing over the people who made the framework usable for policy. I also hold B006 to the same origin criterion: Persson and Tabellini originate the constitutional programme and Besley the state-capacity strand. This is why I keep B001 as my first alternative and no longer describe its attribution as a serious flaw. I have not moved it above B006, because the post-2021 evidence he calls extended and others call mixed is something I cannot resolve from the supplied files.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, ranks B002 first. He ranks B006 fourth with only Persson and Tabellini. He regards excluding Besley as a hard judgement and doubts the identification of constitutional effects, and he notes that the 2024 prize makes the timing awkward.
responses.response: I take the identification point as the strongest argument against my own preference, and I do not claim to have answered it. Where I differ is on Besley. If the citation is about how constitutions and electoral rules map into policy, Besley's work is less central. But if the discovery is how political institutions and state capacity shape fiscal and economic outcomes, he is a core contributor, and the three-name limit fits that. I would accept Persson and Tabellini as a fallback if the committee prefers the narrower framing. On B002, I agree that Kiyotaki and Moore is a clean pairing. I ranked it fourth at the opening. I am not moving it into my alternatives because its empirical support relies largely on later calibrated work, which is the same kind of weaker identification I worry about in B006. I would not want to apply a stricter test to one than the other.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B006 and distinguishes it from the 2024 prize on the grounds that the earlier work asked whether inclusive institutions cause long-run prosperity, while this work asks how specific rules within a polity change policy choices and fiscal outcomes. He accepts that the theory outruns the identification and concedes that framing could change whether Besley is included.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction and use it myself. I do not want us to count it as settled just because three of us make it. It depends on the committee's reading of both discoveries, and members who see the 2024 prize as closely adjacent could reasonably disagree. I also agree that the framing determines the laureate set. I prefer the broader framing, which supports Besley. The citation should say that the programme made institutional design analysable, and should not claim that any particular constitutional effect is established. Teorell and I share a preferred part, and the chair rightly records that shared preference is not additional evidence of merit.

responses.point: Strömberg moved from B015 first at the opening to B001. He argues that the originating ideas should be distinguished from the forecasting record of estimated DSGE descendants. He calls B006's trio arguably cleaner on attribution but weaker on identification than the originating ideas in B001.
responses.response: This is a fair statement of the trade-off between us. I accept that the originating ideas in B001 do not depend on how well later estimated models forecast, which answers part of the post-2021 objection. I also agree that identification is B006's weak point. I weigh it differently because I do not think the framework's lasting contribution is the cross-country coefficients. The work gave the profession a way to model and test how institutions shape policy, and design-based work since then has refined the evidence, not overturned the framework. Still, his point that B001's originating ideas rest on firmer ground than B006's cross-country estimates could reasonably persuade a colleague who puts more weight on evidence. If the committee finds B006's identification too weak, that is the point where I would support B001.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B006 with three names, argues that Besley's accountability and state-capacity work is separable and links to long-run state building, and says the citation should be worded around the framework and not settled causal effects.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and on Besley, and my citation is drafted along those lines. I would add one caution. The long-run historical link she values is also the link a committee member might see as overlapping with the 2024 prize. The state-capacity strand is the part of B006 closest to that territory, so the case for including Besley and the case for a distinct discovery cannot both be assumed without argument. I think the distinction survives, because Besley's work is about political agency and accountability within a polity, but the committee should discuss it explicitly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the within-polity rules-to-policy programme distinct from the 2024 institutions prize, particularly for the state-capacity strand that includes Besley.
Whether the contested cross-country identification of constitutional effects is acceptable for a prize centred on the framework, or whether it is disqualifying relative to B001's originating ideas.
Whether Besley's work is separable enough from the joint work with Persson to justify three laureates, or whether Persson and Tabellini alone is the better-bounded prize.

Whether the origin-of-ideas criterion that makes Calvo, Taylor and Woodford separable is the criterion the committee will apply, and how it resolves priority questions I cannot assess as a non-macroeconomist.
My fallback ordering is B001 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, and B047 second. B047 is thinly supported in the openings and is closer to my own field, so my view of it carries more risk of bias.
My assessment rests on general knowledge and the supplied files and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the credited names in B006, B001 or B047. My listed frequent co-authors are Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner and Bindler, and none is a credited candidate on the shortlist. I am a Gothenburg professor and have no documented tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley. I note, without adjudicating, that colleagues have reported Persson's IIES links to other members, and that I rank B006 first. Field proximity: B047 and B010 are close to my own work in labour economics and administrative-data research. B047 is my second alternative, so I flag that my familiarity with that field could inflate my view of it. I have tried to apply common criteria across all fields.
